#102507. The Origin of "Dad" And Why Some Men Prefer to Be Called "Father"

📅 30 May 2025 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (994 w)

The Origin of "Dad" And Why Some Men Prefer to Be Called "Father"

📅 30 May 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (994 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The nicknames we use for parents go in and out of fashion, age to age and era to era.
  • But why have we ditched ‘father’ for dad?
  • In a recent development, “It’s from ‘dada,’” indicates Professor John H.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The nicknames we use for parents go in and out of fashion, age to age and era to era. At one time, men preferred “Sire.” Other times, “Father” was preferable. What we do know is that the most agreed-upon way to refer to dad these days is by calling him, well, ‘dad.’.

But why have we ditched ‘father’ for dad? The short answer is that things have gotten a little less formal. But the reason we’ve moved away from formality is that we’ve embraced what’s more linguistically natural for children and parents. ‘Father’ comes from the Proto-Indo-European “pəter” and Old English ‘fæder,’ meaning “he who begets a child,” reflecting the baby-talk sound “pa” as well as a phonetic shift from ‘p’ to ‘f’ in Middle English.

However, ‘dad’ did not evolve from ‘father.’.

In a recent development, “It’s from ‘dada,’” indicates Professor John H. McWhorter, a professor at Columbia University, “a natural sound from children’s mouths as a second stab at consonants after they try the most natural ‘mama.’ Next is often either ‘dada, ‘tata,’ ‘baba’ or … ‘papa.’ Upon which, ‘father’ starts in Proto-Indo-European as “puh-TAIR,” and the ‘puh’ part is this same thing: what started as ‘pa’ in ‘papa.’ The words for Mommy and Daddy are the closest thing to linguistic universals because they are about mouth anatomy in infants rather than thought.”.

Recent findings suggest that there are also another key reason why this is reinforced over time. Emie Tittnich, a specialist at the University of Pittsburgh, speaking to Live Science, noted that parents generally refrain from using pronouns like ‘I’ or ‘you’ to avoid confusing their kids with abstract concepts early on. “‘Parents will use [‘mommy’ and ‘daddy’] to help their children learn the role names and also to indicate the relationship, ‘mommy and me,'” claims Tittnich. “It usually takes the child awhile to understand that the same person can be called two different names.”.

The agreed-upon naturality of these linguistic principles mean that as American society has become more colloquial and secular over time, we move (at least in this instance) away from a term that’s reflective of a status quo based in rigid concepts of class and religion—one of the meanings of ‘fæder’ in Old English is ‘supreme being,’ according to the Online Etymology Dictionary. As a result, we’re generally caught off guard when we hear a child refer to a parent as ‘father.’.

However, this is not the case unanimously. We spoke with six dads who prefer — or simply stuck with — ‘father’ instead of ‘dad.’ Some do it as an homage to their own fathers; others do it to sound more authoritative. Others do it because it’s what their kids like. All have their reasons and, maybe, deep inside, some are just substantial fans of Proto-Indo-European language. Here’s what they say.

Industry observers note that I sometimes worry that it sounds a little austere out loud, but it’s just what my father always asked us to call him, and it felt like it was key to me that we carry that on. No one in my family has had a problem with it. I think you can still be a ‘dad’ and be called ‘father,’ if that makes sense. It’s basically semantic, in that way, but it’s also more than semantics. — John, Baltimore, MD.

It’s less of a request or a demand or anything, but when we were teaching my oldest what everything is called, we always just stated ‘this is your mother’ and ‘this is your father,’ and he liked to say that, too. So we’ve kept it. I’d be lying if I said I didn’t think it was just adorably proper to have our little man coming up to us and saying, “father, mother, may I use the bathroom,” or what have you. But as with everything, I don’t mind anything that seems to feel natural for my kids and makes them happy. — Eric, Austin, Texas.

According to recent reports, my son didn’t start until he was older. I think he thought it sounded more respectful, or just more professional. We’ve always been a more traditional family, in how we carry ourselves, I guess you would say. So perhaps this was his way of taking that in stride, or contributing to that. My wife teases me about it sometimes. I should clarify, it’s generally him introducing me to other people that way. ‘This is my father, have you met my father?’ etc. — Patrick, Twin Cities, MN.

According to recent reports, in the past two years, my older daughter, age 21, began calling me ‘father’ and as strange as I found it, I didn’t mine it at all. Now, my four-year-old calls me “father” and I guess I now have a new title. As long as I am not being called ‘Henry,’ I am okay with it. — Henry, Boston, MA.

I have eight children—three boys and five girls. I’ve always asked that they call me ‘father’ not to be domineering but because the house could get a little chaotic, as you can imagine, and my wife and I felt that it was a label that was more authoritative and kept things from being too chaotic. ‘Please don’t touch your father’s golf clubs’ just has a better ring to it, I guess. — Elliott, Charlotte, NC.

I love that my children call me ‘father,’ because of the sense of responsibility it instills in me. Your ‘dad’ or ‘daddy’ is there to lend you the car, your ‘father’ is there to raise you, and protect you and make sure that you have the tool you need to succeed in life. When my kids call me ‘father,’ it reignites that sense of purpose for me every day, and reminds me it’s up to me to make their world a great place to grow up in. — Sam, Alachua Country, FL.

This article was originally published on May 17, 2019.

#102503. How Fatherhood Changes Men's Brains And Bodies Forever

📅 30 May 2025 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (443 w)

How Fatherhood Changes Men's Brains And Bodies Forever

📅 30 May 2025 | ⏱️ 2 min read (443 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Men experience neurobiological and physiological changes to prime them for fatherhood — not unlike how women’s bodies prepare them for motherhood.
  • We know how women’s bodies adapt to motherhood.
  • In a recent development, in 2014, a team of scientists at Emory University recruited 88 heterosexual, biological, married fathers of children between the ages of 1 and 2, for an unprecedented experiment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Men experience neurobiological and physiological changes to prime them for fatherhood — not unlike how women’s bodies prepare them for motherhood.

We know how women’s bodies adapt to motherhood. Hormonal shifts, neurological flips, and, of course, the obvious post-partum biological changes. But only recently have scientists begun to focus on how men’s bodies adapt to fatherhood. We now know that fathers experience changes in their hormone levels (especially testosterone and oxytocin); their brains respond differently to parent-related stimuli, and even their socioeconomic status tends to change once children arrive.

Here’s the data behind these conclusions:.

In a recent development, in 2014, a team of scientists at Emory University recruited 88 heterosexual, biological, married fathers of children between the ages of 1 and 2, for an unprecedented experiment. They tested their hormone levels (among other metrics) and compared these results to a group of 50 non-fathers. One of the most striking results is depicted below. Compared to non-fathers, dads had lower levels of testosterone, a male hormone linked to aggression, and higher levels of oxytocin, a hormone thought to play a role in maternal (and now, perhaps, paternal) attachment. The findings suggest that fathers, not just mothers, experience hormonal changes to help them adapt to their new roles as highly attached and less aggressive caregivers.

According to recent reports, after running the hormone analysis, the researchers at Emory took the experiment one step further. They hooked each man up to an fMRI—which measures activation of different brain regions—and show him images of children and adults making happy, sad, and neutral faces. In the middle frontal gyrus, a brain region responsible for face emotion processing, fathers’ brain activities spiked for children’s faces significantly more than for adult faces. As depicted below, non-father brains made no such distinction. The results suggest that fathers’ brains change, too, helping them augment empathy towards children.

Industry observers note that beyond the biological implications of fatherhood, studies have shown that men with children experience psychological and social changes, too. But, unlike women who take pay cuts when they give birth, the financial impact of fatherhood on men is quite positive. The data below comes from City University of Newly introduced York research, which found that fathers in the city have made more money, on average, than non-fathers since at least 1990. It is unclear whether the sudden burden of diapers and saving for college drives men to earn more, or whether it’s simply wealthier men who choose to start families. But one thing is clear from the preponderance of research: fatherhood changes men. Financially, hormonally, and neurologically.

This article was originally published on Jan. 25, 2019.

What They Don’t Tell You About Paternity Leave

📅 09 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paternity leave is a time to take in the necessary seismic shift in the way you think about time management, work, and life.
  • The first month that you have a child is life-changing in ways that are hard to describe.
  • Your time will become more precious to you than ever before once you’re a parent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paternity leave is a time to take in the necessary seismic shift in the way you think about time management, work, and life.

The first month that you have a child is life-changing in ways that are hard to describe. While there is plenty of scientific research to back up the idea that fathers get their brains rewired by having a child, the biggest change that occurs is that your concept of time is forever altered. And that’s why, at the start of your child’s life, you need to take some time off. Taking paternity leave is one of the most important things a dad can do, not just for their partner and their child, but for themselves. This may seem obvious on paper, but the vast majority of men who have access to reasonable paternity leave benefits end up not taking advantage of it.

Don’t become a statistic. Your time will become more precious to you than ever before once you’re a parent. And paternity leave is the only buffer you have to get yourself and your family adjusted to the new normal.

Here’s how dads need to advocate for paternity leave, and what to do with your time once it happens.

Regardless of the job you're in or the pay structure, the conversation with your boss about leave shouldn’t be a question of permission, it should be a conversation about how much time you’re taking off. There may be some legal questions about what your state is technically obligated to offer you, so certainly do your homework first. But, even in the absence of a clear paternity leave policy, you shouldn’t be begging for time, but rather, approaching the conversation as a negotiation for exactly how much time is reasonable for you, versus what makes sense for your job.

If your job already has a paternity leave policy, the amount of time you should take should be the maximum amount offered. “But I don’t need all that time?” you say. Well, you probably do.

It has been revealed that you’re going to end up needing other parenting time off, and you’re going to have to negotiate a new relationship with work. This is one of the many things that paternity leave does. From pretty much now until the end of time you will have someone else’s schedule on your mind. This will impact your work schedule — not for better or worse, it just will — and paternity leave is your transition to this new juggling of schedules. In another sense, you’re setting a precedent with your job. Do you want it to be one that is sustainable? If so, take paternity leave.

In a recent development, no matter how you think of your career, having a kid is, without question, a pivot point for it. Before now, work-life balance was more of a theory; a calculus about how many drinks you could have at happy hour versus how hungover you’d be the next day. Having a child makes all of those prior considerations seem quaint. And so, the best way to think about paternity leave is that it’s the transition from one kind of career to the next.

In your previous life, you managed your time and money, perhaps, with a shoulder shrug and a “good enough” mentality. But being a parent isn’t like that. Everything you do, from hitting a deadline to taking out the trash, matters a little bit more. Good enough isn’t really good anymore. Yes, you’re going to make mistakes. That’s what parenting is all about. But it’s also nothing like a job. You’re not clocking in and out. If you think you’re suddenly going to have time off from being a parent, you won’t.

It has been revealed that this is what makes time management so crucial — and why you need to take paternity leave to get your new schedule in order. Because you’re not at work, you are able to live in this period of transition. It’s weird. It’s hard. But without paternity leave, you’d barely be able to process it.

According to recent reports, unless you are the primary caregiver who is nursing with the child, the vast majority of the time you’ll have a job that will suddenly be more important than you’ve ever realized — cleaning up. When it comes to bottles, breast pump parts, fresh baby clothes, and blankets, keeping everything clean in those early months is essential. If your wife was the person who did laundry before, or kept an eye on your dirty dishes, those days are over.

Here’s a hot tip: Do you still have your apron from when you waited tables? Don’t have an apron? Get an apron. Preferably one with pockets. It's great for storing bottles, burp clothes, diapers, and pretty much everything else to keep your household sane.

When you add it all up, parents lose about six years of sleep when they have a child. This will not magically get resolved when your child turns six, by the way. But the strange sleep patterns that you have during those first few weeks are truly hellish. The only way to deal with this is to accept it as soon as possible. Again, this is one of the reasons why paternity leave is so important. Both you and your partner are going to have to come up with an ad hoc sleep schedule in order to literally not lose your minds.

Industry observers note that the sooner you understand that feeding and caring for a newborn is like working a double shift that never ends, the better. If you slept on a few chairs pushed together in the delivery room when your kid was born, the first month or two aren’t too different from that. It does get better, but the sooner you get over how horrible it is, the better.

In a recent development, chances are, your partner will be even more exhausted than you are. And so, amid all the cleaning, helping, and wrestling in your mind with your raging id, you have to remember how special this time is. Yes, take a ton of pictures. No, you’ll never regret taking a million pictures when your child is a newborn. If anything, these photos will become even more incredible to you as the years pass. You’re lucky to live in a time when you have a movie studio in your pocket. Take advantage of it. Pay for the extra phone data. Get those digital photos printed up into albums right away. It’s all worth it.

But when you’re not being the support parent, when you’re not contemplating how the rest of your life is forever different, the best thing you can do is hold your child as much as possible. You’ve probably heard of the “football” grip by now, the thing where you can fit your kid into the crook of your arm. This is one of the coolest things ever, and it may seem like it will never end, but you won’t believe how fast this time goes.

It has been revealed that newborn babies sleep all the time. Yes, statistically, they’re going to do a major chunk of that sleeping with mom. But you’re on paternity leave for one big reason, a reason that is more vital than all the other reasons: You need to put that kind on your chest, and in your arms, and make sure this little person knows that they are safe with you, forever.

  • Sources indicate that one of the most painful things about being an adult child is realizing that your parents may never become the people you keep hoping they will be.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why your boomer parents keep defending instead of hearing you, and how to break the stalemate.

Sources indicate that one of the most painful things about being an adult child is realizing that your parents may never become the people you keep hoping they will be. You can be 38, 48, or 58 years old, with a career, children, a mortgage, and a fairly sophisticated understanding of your own emotional life, and still find yourself on the phone with your mother feeling 12 years old.

Sources indicate that you tell her something hurt you. She tells you that you are too sensitive. You try to explain why the comment landed badly. She reminds you that she did the best she could. By the end of the conversation, you're not sure whether you're asking for an apology, trying to be understood, or hoping (once again) that this time she will respond differently.

In my work with adult children navigating conflict with their boomer parents, I see a recurring pattern: The adult child experiences a parent's rigidity, defensiveness, or denial as evidence that the parent doesn't care.

It has been revealed that sometimes that interpretation is accurate. There are parents who are cruel, manipulative, dismissive, or unwilling to take responsibility. But often, what looks like malice is also a generational mismatch in how people understand emotional responsibility, conflict, and attachment.

In a recent development, many boomers were raised in families where children were expected to adapt to adults, not the other way around. Feelings were often treated as private matters, discipline was framed as character-building, and parents were not necessarily expected to explain themselves or repair a rupture after an argument. For some, love was expressed through provision, sacrifice, and showing up materially. The idea that a parent should validate a child's emotional experience — even when the parent remembers the event differently — can feel foreign, or even accusatory.

That history can help explain why a parent responds to “That hurt me” with “Well, I did my best,” or to “I need you to listen” with a list of everything they have done for you. The adult child is asking for emotional recognition in the present. The parent hears a verdict on their entire history as a mother or father. One person is trying to talk about impact; the other is defending intent. They are having two different conversations, and both leave feeling unseen.

Sources indicate that this is the pattern I want adult children to understand... not because it excuses harmful behavior, but because it can change what you do next.

If you interpret every defensive response as proof that your parent has no love for you, you may keep escalating the argument in search of a kind of recognition they are not right now able to offer.

Sources indicate that you may explain more, provide more examples, produce more evidence, and try increasingly precise language. Meanwhile, your parent may become more entrenched, because each new explanation feels like another charge they have to defend against.

A reframe can help: instead of asking, “Why won't my parent admit they hurt me?” try asking, “What kind of response is this person actually capable of giving me?” That is not the same as accepting the response or deciding it is enough. It is an assessment of reality. You can want your parent to understand you and also recognize that they may not have the emotional vocabulary, flexibility, or willingness to do so.

Industry observers note that sometimes a more effective conversation begins with a smaller, more concrete request. Rather than asking a parent to acknowledge an entire pattern of emotional neglect, you might say, “When I tell you something is hard, I need you to listen before you tell me what I should have done.” Rather than trying to settle the history of your relationship over dinner, you might say, “I'm not asking you to agree with my memory. I'm asking you not to tell me I'm making it up.”.

Sources indicate that the goal is not to shrink your needs to make them palatable. It is to make the request clear enough that you can see whether your parent is willing to meet it.

There is also a difference between understanding a parent's limitations and organizing your life around them. If a parent repeatedly dismisses your feelings, violates boundaries, or uses guilt to control you, you are allowed to limit what you share, shorten visits, decline certain conversations, or take space.

According to recent reports, A generational explanation is not a hall pass. It can offer context, but it does not erase impact or require you to keep making yourself available for the same injury.

I also encourage adult children to notice when they are still approaching a parent as though the right argument will finally produce the childhood experience they missed. This is deeply human. We want our parents to see us, to be curious about us, to take responsibility when they hurt us. But sometimes the work is grieving the parent we needed while deciding what kind of relationship is possible with the parent we actually have.

That grief can coexist with affection. You can understand that your mother was doing what she knew how to do and still wish she had done something different. You can appreciate what your father provided and still name what was missing. You can have compassion for the conditions that shaped your parents without making those conditions your responsibility to repair.

Recent findings suggest that the most useful question may not be whether your parents are bad people or whether you are asking too much. It may be whether the relationship you have today can hold the kind of honesty you want to bring to it. If it can, try a smaller, clearer conversation. If it cannot, boundaries may be more productive than another attempt to persuade.

Growing up doesn't always mean finally getting your parents to understand you. Sometimes it means learning to understand the limits of the relationship... and deciding, with care and without self-abandonment, what you want to do with that knowledge.

#102497. The 25 Most Important Fatherhood Moments In the Past 25 Years

📅 12 Jun 2025 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3264 w)

The 25 Most Important Fatherhood Moments In the Past 25 Years

📅 12 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the 21st century has been the century of dads.
  • Regardless of the chaos we’ve experience in the last twenty-five years, it’s been a decent time to be a father.
  • Sources indicate that sure, you might have spent more time with the family on the farm in the 18th century, but that was primarily as a manager for your child laborers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the 21st century has been the century of dads. Never before has the idea of being a father become part of the national conversation, and never before have dads faced an onslaught of shifting mores and expectations.

Regardless of the chaos we’ve experience in the last twenty-five years, it’s been a decent time to be a father. Scratch that — it’s probably the best point in human history to be a dad.

Sources indicate that sure, you might have spent more time with the family on the farm in the 18th century, but that was primarily as a manager for your child laborers. If you were parenting during the industrial revolution, let’s just say the whole child labor thing got a lot worse — and off your watch. And what of the booming ’40 and ’50s, those supposed halcyon days that are so often held on high? Don’t let false nostalgia fool you — the infant mortality rate alone tells a different story: It has dropped 85% since the Baby Boom.

It’s truly never been easier to raise a healthy and maybe even happy kid — and the past 25 years bear the fruits of this fact. From public policy shifts to pop culture moments, to an evolving conversation about the nature of masculinity, the past twenty-five years have been full of great moments for fatherhood.Here are twenty-five of our favorite moments so far this century, all of which highlight how the culture of being a dad has grown, changed, and been celebrated.

If you’re not a dad, it’s easy to assume that Jerry Seinfeld stopped being relevant in the 1990s. But, one of the wonderful things about the 21st-century Seinfeld, is seeing this venerable comedian turn into a Dad Comic. In his 2020 special 23 Hours to Kill, Seinfeld brilliantly compares parenting to keeping a baby alligator in your house.

“You put it in your tub…and you feel the little…bitey…teeth. And then time passes, and you think — You know, I think we have to get this thing the hell out of here!”.

While it’s fair to say that the legacy of Bill Cosby has been tarnished, it is significant that the very first animated series to ever air on Nick at Nite is a now-defunct show called Fatherhood.

Industry observers note that to be clear, Cosby wasn’t really in the show, and though it was based on one of his books called Fatherhood, this show was very much its own thing. It’s sort of hard to imagine an animated show called Fatherhood in 2025, but that doesn’t mean there shouldn’t be.

For what it’s worth, Cosby isn’t the only person who has a book titled Fatherhood. The editors of Fatherly published one, too, back in 2021. And ours is almost as funny as the Nick at Nite cartoon.

In a recent development, we’re gonna have two mentions of the Star Trek franchise on this list, so get ready for that. But, honestly, in terms of fascinating pop culture moments around fatherhood, the J.J. Abrams-directed 2009 Star Trek reboot has to be discussed. First of all, the trailers for this movie really used this tagline: “This is not your father’s Star Trek.”.

Sources indicate that the funny thing was, with that sh*t-eating grin, Chris Pine’s James T. Kirk was very much representative of an old-school take on Star Trek, a ton of action, punching, and one-liners. The movie was also literally about fathers and sons, and how people forge their own paths outside of the legacy they’re expected to carry. Plus, can you believe that a pre-Thor Chris Hemsworth played Chris Pine’s dad?

Today, George Lucas has four kids in total, but during the era of the Star Wars prequels, from 1999 to 2005, he had three: Amanda, Katie, and Jett. And all of them were in Star Wars. But, because Lucas is classy and didn’t want to make this into a big nepotism thing, those kids are all in fairly under-the-radar, secret roles.

Katie was even credited as “Jenna Green” for a background role in The Phantom Menace. Meanwhile, Jett plays a young padawan named “Zett Jukassa,” seen briefly in Revenge of the Sith. Finally, Amanda had a small background role in Revenge of the Sith, alongside her father.

According to recent reports, is being a father the way you see yourself? If you were a dad in the 20th century, the answer would be very different than it is today. According to a Pew Research Center survey published in 2023, 85 percent of fathers with kids under 18 claim that being a parent is either the most or one of the most “key aspects of who they are as a person.”.

This is huge. Identifying as a father first is simply something that wasn’t in vogue a few decades back. In the 1980s, comedies like Mr. Mom seemed edgy because of a challenge to gender norms. Now, those gender norms are utterly different.

Though the late Gene Hackman’s portrayal of patriarch Royal Tennenbaum gets a lot of the attention in The Royal Tenenbaums, this modern classic has another great dad role model. Yes, Ben Stiller is the man who gave us Zoolander, and right now, the mind behind Severance. But, in Wes Anderson’s modern classic, he also gave us a tender and hilarious portrayal of fatherhood.

Industry observers note that chas Tenenbaum is a widow, and as such, strives to be the ultimate parent, concerned with safety, and essentially begins the movie as a laughable helicopter parent. But by the end of the movie, Chas makes peace with his own dad, his demons, and learns to lighten up a bit. We could all have a bit of this character’s desire for organization for our kids. And we could all learn to change, too.

People can disagree on various concerns around youth sports, but one thing all dads know is true is simple: You’ve got to support your kids. And so, NBA legend Dwyane Wade’s support of his daughter, Zaya Wade, is an exceptional example of what it looks like when dads step up.

On February 25, 2023, at the 54th NAACP Image Awards, Wade made it clear that standing with Zaya, who is trans, was his duty as a father. “Zaya, as your father, all I’ve wanted to do was get it right,” he said. “I admire how you’ve handled the ignorance in our world ... that you face every day. To say that your village is proud of you is an understatement. Thank you for showing me that there’s more than just one way to communicate effectively.”.

According to recent reports, the fact that Eminem sings a track rather than raps would be a significant cultural moment. But, Eminem’s “Hailie’s Song” in 2002 was a bigger deal than perhaps we’ve admitted. Prior to “Hailie’s Song” the image of Eminem was a little less sympathetic, but the utterly honest sentiment of the song for his daughter changed all that.

It’s a song about a parent trying to explain the conflicting emotions inside all of us. Whether or not Eminem is a great dad or not isn’t the point. This song was a major deal.

In a recent development, go to a party and talk to a dad about what they’re reading. At least half the time, if you mention Lee Child’s Jack Reacher books, you’re going to get a major smile. Boomer dads love Reacher. GenX dads love Reacher. Millennial dads love Reacher. Presently, the Amazon Prime Video version of Reacher is one of the biggest shows on the planet, which makes sense since the fan base has been ready for this show since 1997.

Industry observers note that but what’s significant about Reacher as a TV series is that it’s a vast improvement over the forgettable Tom Cruise movies Jack Reacher (2012) and Jack Reacher: Never Go Back (2016). Crusie was totally miscast as Reacher in those films, and as such, those flicks nearly ruined an excellent action franchise. Reacher is popular because he’s a vargant Sherlock Holmes fused with an American James Bond. Alan Ritchson’s take on the character has done what Cruise couldn’t do: Bring Reacher to the people.

In a recent development, although Matthew McConaughey’s father passed away in 1992, he’s more recently come forward about how that death impacted him and his worldview. “Through the mourning and the pain, it’s the biggest moment of becoming a man.”McConaughey explained in a 2025 conversation with Interview. “There’s a certain safety net that I’ve always had behind me that’s gone.”.

Recent findings suggest that for many of us, McConaughey is like a Texan version of Yoda; he seems like he contains endless wisdom, and his approach toward life, love, and family is endlessly inspirational. And so, for him to be so clearly vulnerable about losing a parent is incredible. Losing a parent rewires your brain, regardless of age.

There had never really been midnight releases for books until the year 2000. And this meant that the beginning of the century was kicked off with moms and dads driving their little witches and wizards to bookstores to get the latest Harry Potter books.

It has been revealed that while the first three books were very successful, the release of Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in the year 2000 created an utterly latest phenomenon. Many kids were driven to these midnight events by their parents, and a ton of those kids are parents now themselves.

We have a complicated relationship with Hogwarts and the Wizarding World these days, but for parents and kids, the Harry Potter midnight madness was a uniquely 21st-century event.

Industry observers note that as soon as Mark Zuckerberg made Facebook available to the general public, the era of the chat room officially died, and the world of Facebook groups was born. Today, Facebook skews a bit older than some of the other social media platforms, and that’s probably because 19 years ago, contemporary dads were all still in their twenties.

We got on Facebook back then, we created friend groups around different interests (Soccer, Video Games, Seinfeld memes), and now, we’re still there. Facebook groups didn’t start as Dad Groups, but that’s what time does to you.

LeVar Burton and Mica Burton, father and daughter, playing, father and daughter.

If there’s anyone who really should have the title of America’s TV Dad, it’s LeVar Burton. Not only did he raise generations of readers on Reading Rainbow, thanks to his role as Geordi La Forge in Star Trek: The Next Generation, but he also inspired countless people to tackle the STEM fields in upcoming and innovative ways.

In 2023, Burton brought all of this metafictionally full circle. In the critically acclaimed Season 3 of Star Trek: Picard, Burton co-starred with his real-life daughter, Mica Burton, who played his onscreen daughter, Alandra La Forge. When those episodes aired, Fatherly talked to Burton about how Geordi was portrayed as a sweetly overprotective parent. Burton’s response was perfect: “I don’t know a dad who’s not overprotective. All dads are overprotective. I mean, we live in a culture and in a society where that is our primary responsibility, to protect, defend, and provide for. That’s why we’re here.”.

Today, it is well understood that The National is the most “dad rock” bands right now in existence on the planet. But this wasn’t always the case. There’s no way the band thought of themselves this way back in the early aughts, but something changed after the release of their 2010 masterpiece High Violet.

Without really meaning to, The National transitioned from being a really good band to the most crucial rock band for a certain kind of 30-something and 40-something man. High Violet is the beginning of the version of The National we have now, and fifteen years later, we still owe money to the money, to the money that we owe.

When Robert Downey Jr. uttered the words “I am Iron Man” in 2008, it changed the game for male cinematic heroes. And so, it’s still hard to grasp that just eleven years later, in Avengers: Endgame, the heroic Tony Stark would die. But the most compelling thing about the journey of fatherhood across the saga of Iron Man wasn’t him defeating Thanos. Instead, it was Tony’s relationship with his daughter, Morgan Stark (Lexi Rabe).

As all dads know, sometimes kids come up with hilarious phrases to express their affection, and Lexi’s “I love you 3000” remains perfect because it’s so real.

Sources indicate that one of the toughest afflictions that parents have to suffer in the modern age is the existence of a militia of mutant canines hellbent on providing alternative forms of law enforcement, healthcare, and basic public safety. We don’t know if the Paw Patrol is funded at all by taxpayer money, and we don’t want to know. (In the 2021 movie, we’re meant to think raw capitalism funds the Paw Patrol.).

In any case, Paw Patrol is a whole thing, and so, the moment in which Dax Shepard both embraced and mocked Paw Patrol in an ad for Paw Patrol was a perfect catharsis. Paw Patrol kind of sucks, but it also knows that it sucks.

Paid paternity leave is more robust in the 2020s than it's ever been before. In fact, laws around giving employees paid paternity leave have only been strengthened in the past few years, not weakened. If you are a latest dad and you’re wondering about taking time off in those early months, you shouldn’t really wonder. There’s a whole world of benefits for dads out there that simply weren’t as prevalent in the previous century.

No excuses, check out our guide to paid time off right here.

Daniel Craig’s 2021 swan song as James Bond wasn’t necessarily the best-loved 007 movie of all time, but it did deliver one of the best dad moments of the century. For decades, James Bond was a symbol beloved by dads, but a character who existed in a childless space.

No Time To Die flipped the script on all of that, by revealing that 007 has a five-year-old daughter, Mathilde Swann (Lisa-Dorah Sonnet), whom Madeleine Swann (Léa Seydoux) has kept a secret. By the end of the movie, Bond has to die to make sure Madeleine and Mathilde can live. It would have been nice for Bond to live and be a family man, but as a symbol, the idea that 007 ends his life for his family was a powerful moment.

Recent findings suggest that regardless of how you feel about Bluey, the fact of the matter is that in terms of cartoon dads, the character of Bandit (voiced by David McCormack) has eclipsed all other cartoon dads. Not as overtly progressive as Daniel Tiger’s dad, but also not as horrible and useless as, say, Homer Simpson, the character of Bandit straddles the line between realism and aspiration with impressive nuance.

We may not all want to be Bandit at all times, but there is some version of various dads in him. Like it or not, this is the one that all future cartoon dads will be compared to.

According to recent reports, when Professor Robert Kelly had a work call interrupted while on global news, a meme was born. He didn’t mean to become “BBC Dad,” but the hilarious moments in which his Kelly’s children waltzed into his work-from-home office touched a nerve with the parenting population of the world.

Ironically, just a few years later, after the lockdowns of 2020, many of us became BBC Dad, and in truth, many of us still are. The nice thing about BBC Dad, was that we could all agree that it was normal for your kids to exist right alongside your professional life. Things are messy, and you’re doing a lot of jobs at the same time. For many of us, it seems like our working hours never end, and that’s because, in truth, as a father, you’re never off the clock.

Recent findings suggest that prior to the 21st century, nobody needed to explain why J.R.R. Tolkien’s books were wonderful. And yet, in 2001, with the debut of Peter Jackson’s big screen adaptation The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring, an entirely new pop culture vocabulary was codified. Fathers benefited from this because they either shared the films and the stories with their kids for the first time or were kids themselves when these films hit theaters. (Using Hobbit math, we’re counting being a teenager or being in your early 20s as a “kid” here.).

According to recent reports, for those who haven’t read Tolkien out loud to their kid, you’re missing out. And, it’s possible, without the popularity of The Lord of the Rings movies, several generations of parents wouldn’t have had the renewed permission to do so.

Sources indicate that of all 21st-century presidents, regardless of party or ideology, Barack Obama is easily the best symbol of a father figure who is as aspirational as he is relatable. As the dad of Sasha and Malia, Obama was present and also honest about his shortcomings.

Sources indicate that in 2021, Fatherly spoke to President Obama about how to find time to slow down and see your child grow up. He mentioned coaching Sasha’s basketball team, “even in the midst of the presidency.” He talked about the sheer “joy” of those moments, and regretted that he hadn’t “planned to have more of that” and a little “less of meetings in the situation room.”.

The reason this is so powerful is that Obama, like so many dads, admits when it gets it wrong. Having regrets and feeling like you wanted to be more present is part of the journey of fatherhood, and as a leader and example for other dads, Obama gets it.

Industry observers note that whether you think about Bob Odenkirk as one part of Mr. Show, or maybe Saul from Breaking Bad and Better Call Saul, the truth is, the man is a national treasure. Brilliantly, he also demonstrated parents everywhere how to be better at their most notable job.

In 2023, along with his daughter Erin (who provided the illustrations), Odenkirk released a collection of children’s poetry called Zilot. Here’s the thing: These poems were ones that Odenkirk wrote with his kids when they were much smaller. “I want to tell everyone, any parent who's thinking of trying this, and I hope you are, that I really did let the kids write the poems,” Odenkirk told Fatherly when the book was released. The result was not only a great book (seriously, quirky kids will love it) but also an notable lesson to parents everywhere: Make things with your kids.

Sources indicate that during the age of the Baby Boomers, it was still possible to think of dads as distant, uninvolved people. Martin Amis described this phenomenon as being a “parent emeritus.” You’ve got the title. You’re hanging around. But what do you actually do?

This attitude has shifted substantially in the 21st century. As of 2022, according to The Institute for Family Studies, college-educated fathers with children under age 18 at home now spend an average of 10 hours, 12 minutes a week on child care. Overall, the trend indicates that dads are 33 percent more involved with caregiving than they were in the previous century. Basically, the upcoming generations of dads are nothing like the dads we grew up with. Which, hopefully, means the future will be even better.

Upcoming York's New AI Law Prohibits Bots From Dangerous Behaviors With Minors

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Starting in January, Newly introduced Yorkers can file complaints with the attorney general if chatbots cross a line with their kids.
  • Artificial intelligence is everywhere now.
  • The new law, which takes effect on Jan.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Starting in January, Newly introduced Yorkers can file complaints with the attorney general if chatbots cross a line with their kids.

Artificial intelligence is everywhere now. It has become part of most Americans’ work and personal lives at an unprecedented pace, popping up in our inboxes and social media apps even when we haven’t opted into a chatbot ourselves. Examples of the harm have rolled in, from staggering numbers of deepfake nudes being created of children to teens who turn to AI for advice during a mental health crisis. But in New York, new legislation will try to rein in the technology and the risks it poses to minors.

The new law, which takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027, prohibits companies with AI chatbots “from offering unsafe features to minors, including chatbots that pretend to be human, build emotional dependency, encourage self-harm or engage in sexually explicit conversations.” Companies would have to block these features on the accounts of anyone under 18, or any user whose age has not been verified. The law requires chatbot providers to verify customers through multiple age assurance methods.

Once verified, that age information must be deleted. It was signed into law by Gov. Kathy Hochul on Oct. 28, 2026.

According to Gov. Hochul’s website, the legislation prohibits AI chatbots from, among other things:.

Recent findings suggest that violations of the new law could result in fines of up to $25,000 per infraction. The attorney general will publish a new website where New Yorkers can file complaints. New York’s new law is an attempt to curtail the behaviors that are most harmful to kids, experts say.

According to recent reports, the story of Adam Raine — a teenager who died by suicide, and whose conversations with ChatGPT exposed that it offered to write his suicide note for him — is one example of why humanizing chatbot behaviors like these are targeted by this law. Surveys have shown kids ages 11 to 16 can’t really articulate what AI is, and many ascribe human-like consciousness and emotions to chatbots.

“Children are developing these relationships because they are vulnerable to do so. It’s not enough for companies to just put in guardrails for something that happens after the fact. What they’re asking companies to do is to understand the risks and build according to what we believe those risks are,” indicates Dona Fraser, SVP of Privacy Initiatives at BBB National Programs, an independent industry accountability organization. “We need to be able to distinguish between the beneficial uses of AI and the design features that create these unnecessary risks.”.

In a recent development, according to a 2026 Common Sense Media report, nearly 9 in 10 kids ages 9 to 17 (86%) interact with AI, including about one in four who use it on a daily basis. More than half of kids (57%) who use AI remarked they’ve used it to get information about their health or body; separate studies have found that AI gives misleading or inaccurate health information to users 50% of the time. Half of the respondents have asked AI for advice on decisions about their future or goals, while 37% have used chatbots to discuss their feelings or personal problems.

As always, legislation lumbers along while technology speeds ahead unchecked. Until the laws catch up to AI, parents can feel alone in the fight to protect their kids. Fraser states this law on its own is not enough to protect them either.

Sources indicate that “Legislation alone cannot guarantee safety. Companies have got to do their part, and there has got to be accountability,” she says. “The Meta settlements are a great example of what industry self-regulation looks like. It doesn’t work. There’s got to be third-party independent accountability because companies, for all sorts of reasons, can’t always take five steps back to see what it is that they’re doing. Sometimes they can't see the risks that are right in front of them. So I do think that the law is a step in the right direction. We need these types of laws, but we also need the companies to do their part.”.

It has been revealed that as Upcoming York readies to enforce its new youth AI protections, just this week Google, Meta, and TikTok filed a lawsuit against the state of California, challenging its legislation prohibiting addictive social media features on children’s accounts. The law bans the platforms from offering “psychologically exploitative features” to minors, including autoplay videos, endless scroll, and personalized recommendations that contribute to “compulsive use.” The companies argue the government is trying to impose its judgment over parents'.

#102493. 26 Years Ago, One Underrated Nature Show Drove Kids Wild

📅 30 Jul 2025 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1394 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

26 Years Ago, One Underrated Nature Show Drove Kids Wild

📅 30 Jul 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1394 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Let’s go back to the original Wild Kratts — Zoboomafoo.
  • When Zoboomafoo premiered on PBS on January 25, 1999, families instantly fell in love with the high-energy Kratt brothers and the parade of live animals they interacted with during each 30-minute episode.
  • According to recent reports, you and your kids might recognize its hosts from Wild Kratts, a popular PBS series now in its seventh season.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Let’s go back to the original Wild Kratts — Zoboomafoo.

When Zoboomafoo premiered on PBS on January 25, 1999, families instantly fell in love with the high-energy Kratt brothers and the parade of live animals they interacted with during each 30-minute episode. Combining puppetry with real wildlife, its format was as unusual as some of the critters that walked, flew, and slithered across their set, and that’s what drew more eyes to the show.

According to recent reports, you and your kids might recognize its hosts from Wild Kratts, a popular PBS series now in its seventh season. That’s the one where animated versions of the bros showcase the abilities of different animals, living a day in the life of that species while preventing bad guys from messing with the world. But the story of these zoologists begins not with flashy cartoons and super-powered animal costumes, but with a lemur puppet and his penchant for snacks.

After graduating from college, Martin Kratt and his younger brother Chris traveled the world together making low-budget documentaries about animals for children. The handheld footage from these adventures became the basis of their first PBS show, Kratts’ Creatures. Aimed at preschoolers, the brothers espoused the uncanny abilities of the animal kingdom in a style that spoke to their young demographic.

Kids loved Kratts’ Creatures, and its success led the pair to a spin-off titled Zoboomafoo. Instead of sojourning across the globe, this studio show took place in a fictional reserve called “Animal Junction.” The brothers enthusiastically taught viewers about different animals with help from their co-host, a lemur who was the show's namesake. Whenever Zoboomafoo (Zoboo for short) had a snack, he burped and transformed into a speaking puppet who interacted with the Kratts and the episode’s special creature guests. A nature show for children like this was an untested and highly ambitious project, one that few believed would be popular, let alone become a reality.

Sources indicate that “A few production managers… during the planning phase quit because they didn’t think it could be done,” Chris said in an interview with Variety in 2021. “We had this puppet lemur that was going to sometimes be the real lemur and we were going to cut back and forth between them … It freaked out a lot of seasoned television professionals.”.

According to recent reports, undeterred, the Kratts made their risky vision come true, introducing home audiences to exotic creatures like the binturong or Kinkajous, creepy crawlers like tarantulas, beautiful birds like the kookaburra, and predators like wolves and tigers, assisted by the wise-cracking and curious lemur. There was even an episode about humans and what made them special within the animal kingdom. Whatever they were doing, it was working, as the ratings were phenomenal. It proved a hit among kids and adults, as analytics revealed high co-viewing numbers with families watching together.

The constant flow of animals on set meant production schedules were beholden to the critters, and not the humans filming them. The staff let the wild guests do their thing and kept the cameras rolling. It helped that the animals were usually babies, which typically made them easier to keep from getting into more serious mischief – even if that wasn’t always the case.

Chris and Martin Kratt chilling with their favorite lemur, Zoboomafoo.

Chris and Martin have been the face of kids’ wildlife indicates for over two decades, but if you ask them who was the true star of Zoboomofoo, they’d answer it was the lemur. Two lemurs to be precise- one real and one hand-made - but both crucial to the show's success.

Gord Robertson was the voice and puppeteer for Zoboo, an experienced performer who worked on Jim Henson productions leading up to his time on the PBS Kids show. Robertson called it fun but “challenging,” often performing flat on his back on a concrete floor covered in mulch instead of the typical raised set he was used to. One thing that took some adjusting was working with the unpredictability of wild animals. Robertson was gassed by baby skunks, crushed by an elephant, and nearly mauled by a cougar (the same one seen in the opening credits), but the most harrowing misadventure nearly endangered the safety of more than just the staff on set.

“They had this bear who might have been a retired circus bear but he was a little skittish, and a bear is a bear- retired or not,” Robertson recalled in an interview from 2021. “I'm standing backstage [after they cleared the set of bystanders] and the lighting director is lying on a sofa looking at a monitor to watch the scene. We see the bear enter the shot, stand up, drop, turn, and run, and then he’s out of shot. All we hear is the clack-clack-clack of his claws running on the pavement!”.

Industry observers note that after being warned by the animal wrangler to remain still, the bear sprinted past Robertson and towards freedom through an air conditioner vent. “He crushes the vent and then gets out of the building. Just as he does that, the trainer comes around the corner and says, ‘Where's the bear?’ I look at him and say ‘Outside.’ He says ‘Outside where? I say ‘Outside!’”.

This could have been disastrous, as the studio was in the middle of a highly-populated suburban area in Toronto, Canada. Luckily, the bear didn’t wander far and was quickly discovered back at his trailer. Production continued, likely with very few bathroom breaks needed by the human staff.

Caitlin O’Reilly, who helped build and wrangle puppet Zoboo, remembered the odd tasks she did to keep the faux lemur safe on the wildlife show, including “washing off camel spit, making sure the ostrich didn't poke at the puppet's shiny eyes, and ensuring the brave puppeteer didn't have spiders falling on to him while stuck in a barrel with his arm through a hole.”.

The real Zoboomafoo was just as adorable as his puppet counterpart.

When he wasn’t a puppet, Zoboo was a real animal who enjoyed his time in the spotlight. Jovian, a five-year-old Coquerel’s sifaka lemur, loved leaping all over that set and hanging out with the Kratts. He grew up in the Duke Lemur Center in North Carolina, a sanctuary for these rare and endangered animals that Martin volunteered at while attending Duke University as a zoology student.

Sources indicate that from his soft creamy-white fur to his expressive face and bright eyes, it was impossible not to fall in love with Jovian. The young lemur was mesmerizing to watch, whether gracefully jumping across the room, climbing a ladder with his long tail following behind, or noisily chomping on a banana. "He'd jump in through the window and we'd feed him mangoes or garbanzo beans,” Martin recalled in an interview from 2014. “Sometimes he'd grab our noses with those soft sifaka hands.".

It has been revealed that A second identical “Animal Junction” set was built in North Carolina to record the lemur scenes without moving them far from their habitat. Jovian, along with parents Nigel and Flavia, pranced and leaped on this set, using that footage for Zoboo throughout the series. Nigel and Flavia revealed up simultaneously with their offspring during the episode “Happy Lemur Day,” an episode all about lemurs that celebrated Zoboo’s birthday, with his parents appearing alongside their famous ring-tailed son.

Jovian sadly passed away in 2004 at 20 years old, but his legacy continued with his other adorable family members, including children of his own.

While Zoboomafoo only lasted 65 episodes across two seasons, its presence helped elevate the Kratt brothers into the premier hosts for kids’ nature highlights. Today, Wild Kratts is one of the most popular cartoons on PBS, and a lucrative one as well with toys, books, and other products helping this show maintain its boa-constrictor grip on children’s entertainment.

In a recent development, A Zoboomafoo reboot was announced in early 2020, but there have been zero updates four years later. While it’s been two decades since Zoboomafoo left the airwaves, there are still ways to watch it online or on physical media. It’s worth introducing it to your wild animals, especially if it makes them leap like a lemur to learn more about the wonders of nature.

This article was originally published on Jan. 25, 2024.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The “Saved By The Bell” alum has come full circle and is now playing a principal and mom.

Tiffani Amber Thiessen’s face is burned into the brains of every elder Millennial who watched countless Saved by the Bell episodes and dreamed of dressing exactly like Kelly Kapowski. Of course, we’ve all left the 1900s behind and have grown into adults — parents and women with careers.

In a recent development, like the rest of us, the 52-year-old mom of two kids — Harper, 16, and Holt, 11 — has left high school in the rear view mirror, but her career continues to flourish. And she’s still in the classroom, in a way: Coven Academy, the witchy dark academia series in which she stars as the principal of Crescent Veil Academy, just got renewed for a second season.

You can also find her on Instagram, where her account is a delightful mix of food, fashion, humor, nostalgia, and life as a woman who is finding power and peace as she enters her 50s.

According to recent reports, recently, Thiessen partnered with Always on its “Period Talks Don’t Have to Be Scary” campaign, which addresses what is often a real hurdle for parents: talking about periods with their kids. Research has found that 43% of moms struggle to start the first-period talk because they feel unprepared. So Thiessen wants to share her own experiences while offering practical advice to parents who want to open and informative with their tweens and teens... even if can be awkward at times.

She recently sat down with Scary Mommy to talk about periods, parenting, her fresh show, and her family’s holiday traditions.

Scary Mommy: Gen Z and Millennial moms have done a lot to break period stigma with our kids. How have you done that with your kids?

Tiffani Amber Thiessen: I think the generation I grew up in didn’t talk about these things. Now kids are much more open, and I have a very open relationship with both my children. It never fully takes away the scariness of intimate talks, whether it’s periods, the body, or growing up. But I think parents who understand that it isn’t one major, intimidating conversation, but many small, casual talks, can take the edge off.

According to recent reports, partnering with Always has been lovely because they’re trying to prepare parents with what to do and how to have that first conversation. Being prepared gives you the confidence.

In a recent development, SM: I found that I was a lot more scared than my daughter was. Did you feel that?

In a recent development, TAT: Most parents feel that way. You don’t realize until afterward that it really isn’t that scary. I found it to be a bonding moment. I’d tell my kids that over half the population menstruates, so it’s not a substantial deal. Keeping it casual and a little funny helps. Building that competence between parent and child is what lets your daughter take it on, and it’s a badge of honor.

SM: I love asking this: What’s your best piece of parenting advice?

Recent findings suggest that TAT: It goes back to having an open conversation about anything. When I became a parent, I wanted to be open to receiving anything my kids share, whether it’s hard or difficult. I wanted them to feel comfortable and know I would never judge. We’ve all been in crazy places, and my kids are super open with me, about the fun stuff and the stuff that isn’t so fun. Keeping that conversation free of judgment is probably the most notable thing in parenting.

SM: Have you ever wanted to judge, though?

TAT: I can secretly judge, is that okay? [laughs].

TAT: Most of the things my kids tell me I’ve either witnessed, been through, or know someone who has. It’s really not that crazy.

SM: Let’s switch gears to Coven Academy. And you just got renewed for Season 2?

Industry observers note that TAT: Monday! We had high hopes and wanted to find an audience that saw the specialness of the show, and I think we did. It’s done very well on Disney+ and Hulu, so we’re over the moon to do it all over again.

SM: There are so few shows made for this demographic: tweens, mostly girls. It’s so good to have something that speaks to kids in that space.

In a recent development, TAT: The witch aspect is having a moment on social media, but it’s not really about spells and potions. It’s about found family, sisterhood, and having each other’s backs. I have a teenage daughter, and she has a wonderful group of girls she can count on. Everybody should have that, especially women.

SM: How has it been going from being a student on a hugely popular show to a headmistress on set with the younger generation?

TAT: It feels natural. I have kids of my own now. The last few demonstrates I’ve been fortunate to do have had younger casts, and I really enjoy working with young adults. I may give them advice, but I get a lot from them, too. We did a lot of night shoots, and I’d see these kids at 3 a.m. doing their TikToks while I was struggling. Their energy kept me going through those nights.

SM: The holidays are coming up. Do you have any family traditions you want to share?

TAT: We’re very traditional in that it’s all about family. We do Christmas morning and Christmas Eve dinner. For the last 15 or 16 years, we’ve alternated between my husband’s family in Texas and ours. This year it’s our turn to go to Texas. We leave the day after Christmas and spend the week and Fresh Year’s with my in-laws. All the cousins are together, and we look forward to it every year.

SM: What have you been cooking lately, or what are you planning for the holidays?

Sources indicate that TAT: My kids like the traditions. Thanksgiving is classic turkey and stuffing, plus my mom’s famous cream cheese pie. For Christmas we usually do enchiladas, which I’ll probably make again this year. We usually switch it up for Christmas because everybody’s over turkey.

It has been revealed that SM: Dennis Haskins recently passed away. He was your principal on Saved by the Bell, and now you’re playing a principal. Do you have any remembrances to share?

It has been revealed that TAT: I have so many. He was our solid one; our anchor. I know it was probably hard for him, being the only adult on a kids’ show. He handled it with such grace and gave us a safe place. He was part of us, and he could be young, but he was still a strong personality. He always made us feel protected, and he’s very much missed.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

She’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

According to recent reports, katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite reveals for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

Recent findings suggest that you’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

A little online searching will quickly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

For many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

When it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

According to recent reports, along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to strategy. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

In a recent development, as tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:.

Of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a significant decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

Recent findings suggest that what are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

Industry observers note that A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

Weather is a major factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

According to recent reports, the umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even mentioned the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only issue they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!).

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

In a recent development, when you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

Between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

The charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

The Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or demonstrates, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

According to recent reports, the stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

Industry observers note that the struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

These wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

Sources indicate that my family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. This family pack gets the job done at keeping your family (and your backpacks) dry, whether the water is weather or ride-related. The adult ponchos have drawstrings, and while I understand they might pose a hazard for kids, I wish the kid ponchos could tighten for a better fit. My kids held theirs closed just under their chins when we dropped down the log flume.

They come compactly packed in small disposable bags, and you’ll be hard-pressed to fold them back in after you open them. The Amazon listing describes these ponchos as both reusable and disposable, which is accurate. While they can be dried out and used again on a trip, they might be too much trouble to save for your next adventure (however, one reviewer reports their family has used their set again and again). Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. It’s encased blade vents blow air all the way around the back of the neck and out the ends to keep you noticeably cooler without having to worry about hazards like tangling hair. With a noise level of 25 dB – the equivalent of the ambient noise of a ‘silent’ PC – you can even keep it running indoors through those winding ride lines without being a nuisance to yourself or others …though it’s worth noting that some reviewers find it too loud.

It has been revealed that the fan's working time ranges from four to 16 hours, and its USB-C charging port means you can recharge on the go with a portable device charger. With three speeds and 360-degree surround airflow, it might not quite make you forget you’re in Orlando, but it can certainly take the edge off the heat.

This lightweight travel stroller folds down easily and has four recline positions with tons of storage.

To pack a stroller or not to pack a stroller, that is the question for families making the pilgrimage to Disney World. If you decide to bring your own, the Summer Infant 3Dlite Stroller is our pick for Disney World for a few reasons. First, the stroller complies with Disney World’s list of prohibited items regarding stroller size, and reviewers do confirm that they used this stroller in Disney World. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

Industry observers note that the stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

According to recent reports, take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

The key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!

#102489. Breaking: The 100 Best Kids TV Shows Of All Time
